It's a little late for this post, but better late than never. Looking back, it's hard to believe how much can change in just two years. As an international student from Kyrgyzstan, I arrived at De Anza College with big dreams, a lot of uncertainty, and a hope that one day I would be able to transfer to a top university in the United States. Over the next two years, De Anza became much more than a college for me. It became a community and a place where I grew both personally and professionally. I had the privilege of working as an International Student Assistant, where I met students from all over the world and learned how resilient, hardworking, and inspiring international students truly are. I also served as Chair of Marketing in student leadership and helped co-found the first Kyrgyz Club at De Anza College. When transfer season arrived, I applied to only four universities: UC Berkeley, UC Davis, UC Santa Cruz, and UCLA. I was honored to be admitted to UC Berkeley, UC Davis, and UC Santa Cruz, while being waitlisted at UCLA. I was also incredibly grateful to receive the $30,000 Undergraduate Dean's Award from UC Santa Cruz, awarded in recognition of my achievements, accomplishments, and the contributions I could bring to their community. After carefully reading every acceptance letter and reflecting on my goals, I chose UC Berkeley. Today, as I look back on this journey, I realize that the biggest achievement wasn't the admissions results themselves it was the people I met, the community I became part of, and the growth that happened along the way. To the International Student Programs team at De Anza College, my mentors, friends, family, and every international student who shared part of this journey with me: thank you. De Anza College Community college showed me that there is no single path to success. Sometimes the path looks different, but it can still lead to extraordinary places. Go Bears 🐻💙 University of California, Berkeley #UCBerkeley #TransferStudent #CommunityCollege #DeAnzaCollege #InternationalStudents #HigherEducation #StudentLeadership ...more

I found out I was having a daughter right after we closed our pre-seed. My co-founders had already quit their jobs. We had a team whose livelihoods depended on me, and clients whose American dreams depended on Alma . And then: a baby. I remember the panic. What do I do now? I decided to keep going. I'd wanted to build my own company for years, going back to the days I hosted Icons like Dario Amodei in my backyard. And I'd wanted to be a mother for just as long. Both were in my nature. I figured I'd manage. I was wrong. Newborn mom and startup CEO are two of the hardest jobs there are, and I was doing both at once. I cried more times than I can count. I pumped between investor meetings. One day my daughter was sick and wouldn't let go of my hand, so I took my client calls holding her. But the hardest part was never the schedule. It was the guilt. I'd watch other moms talk about the time they spend with their kids, and I'd feel like I was failing. But my husband Chyngyz reframed it for me. He said our daughter won't remember the hours. But she'll grow up watching her mother be resilient, watching how much a woman can carry for the people who depend on her. That's not something I grew up seeing in the culture I come from. It's the whole reason we immigrated to America. So she'll know that in this country, there is nothing she can't achieve and no dream too big to chase. Am I still guilty some days? Yes. But the guilt made me more determined. Every minute away from her is one I owe her to make count. Through Alma I've met so many amazing women who juggle it all, and we don't talk about this part enough. The crying, the guilt, the feeling of failing at both. We perform the easy version and fault ourselves for finding the real one hard. If you're a mom leading at a startup, my DMs are always open. I'd love to know: what's the part nobody warned you about, the part you wish we said out loud more often?

I’m excited to share that this past May, I graduated from University of California, Berkeley with a B.A. in Molecular and Cell Biology, Molecular Therapeutics and a minor in Turkish. During my undergraduate years, I was heavily involved in therapeutic projects using CRISPR at the Innovative Genomics Institute (IGI) and completed my honors thesis in Fyodor Urnov’s lab. I was honored to receive the Best Poster in Molecular Therapeutics Award in the UC Berkeley Department of Molecular and Cell Biology . Doing research at the IGI has truly become a dream come true. It gave me the opportunity to pursue my long standing interest in genome editing. I’m incredibly grateful to have learned from and been part of the teams led by Fyodor Urnov , Matthew Kan , Petros Giannikopoulos , and so many others who have shaped the way I think about science and research. I’ve recently joined the Kleinstiver Lab at the MGB Center for Genomic Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School . I’m excited to continue learning and contributing to the development of genome engineering technologies for research applications and for the treatment of human diseases. Most importantly, I want to thank all of my mentors, lab mates, friends, and family for supporting me throughout this journey. I truly wouldn't be here without you, and I'm excited for what's next! #UCBerkeley #InnovativeGenomicsInstitute #CRISPR #GenomeEditing #MassachusettsGeneralHospital #HarvardMedicalSchool

It is with great honor that I announce my graduation from the University of California, Davis where I earned my bachelor's degree in International Relations with an emphasis on Peace and Security and a minor in Communications. These past four years have been a deeply enriching and transformative experience, and I am incredibly grateful for the people, opportunities, and challenges that shaped me along the way. My studies deepened my passion for global politics, strengthened my appreciation for cross-cultural understanding, and reinforced the importance of building meaningful connections with people from diverse backgrounds and perspectives. Beyond the classroom, I pursued opportunities to serve my campus community through leadership and advocacy. This desire to create a positive impact led me to serve as a Student Senator in ASUCD , where I represented the perspectives of my fellow students, collaborated with campus administration, and worked to identify solutions that supported the needs of the student body. My experience as a senator inspired me to continue seeking opportunities to support students whose perspectives were not always heard. During my senior year at UC Davis, I joined the board of BridgeUSA as the Director of Outreach where I worked to foster constructive dialogue among students with differing perspectives and encourage respectful discussions on current events and political issues. I also served as the Political Director of Davis College Republicans , where I organized political discussions and helped create an environment where students with opinions that differed from the campus majority could participate in conversations that mattered to them. Additionally, I was selected to serve on the Jewish Student Leadership Council, a group of student leaders who acted as a liaison between students and university administration on issues related to campus climate, inclusion, and safety initiatives. I am incredibly grateful for the professors who made learning inspiring, the administrators and staff who supported my growth, the peers who made my experience memorable, and above all, my parents, whose unwavering support made this accomplishment possible.
